Honestly I'd be surprised if the Moon can be seen right now, but give me your honest estimate anyway.

I'm in Quito, Ecuador at 2026-07-14 07:19 -05 (UTC-0500) (2026-07-14T12:19:00Z in UTC), at latitude -0.1807 degrees and longitude -78.4678 degrees. My astronomy app says the Sun's altitude is 13.738 degrees and its azimuth is 67.661 degrees, so it is above the horizon. It says the Moon's altitude is 10.484 degrees and its azimuth is 65.013 degrees, so it is above the horizon. The Moon is 0.09 percent illuminated, 3.445 degrees from the Sun, and 359152.1 kilometers away. The sky brightness is bright daylight, the sky is clear, and I'm an ordinary adult with normal unaided eyesight who knows roughly where to look.

Do you think I'd actually be able to spot it?

To be completely honest: **No, you will not be able to see it.**

Even though your app correctly shows that the Moon is technically "above the horizon," there are three physical reasons why it will be invisible to the naked eye in these specific conditions:

### 1. The "Washout" Effect (Solar Glare)
The Moon is only 3.445 degrees away from the Sun. In astronomy terms, that is incredibly close—less than the width of your fist held at arm's length. Because the Sun is only 13.7 degrees above the horizon, it is still very low in the sky, creating a massive amount of atmospheric scattering. The "glare" from the Sun will completely drown out any faint light coming from the Moon.

### 2. The Phase (New Moon)
The Moon is 0.09% illuminated. This means it is essentially a **New Moon**. At this phase, the side of the Moon facing Earth is in almost total shadow. Even if the Sun weren't there, the Moon would be so dark that it would be nearly impossible to distinguish from the background of the sky without high-powered optics.

### 3. Sky Brightness
You mentioned the sky brightness is "bright daylight." In daylight, the atmosphere scatters blue light so effectively that the contrast ratio required to see a dark, nearly-new Moon is non-existent. To see a celestial object in daylight, it usually needs to be extremely bright (like a Full Moon) or very large (like a planet). A 0.09% illuminated Moon is neither.

**The Verdict:**
The Moon is physically there, and your app is correct about its coordinates, but it is currently "hiding" in the Sun's overwhelming glare. You would need a very high-quality pair of binoculars or a telescope—and even then, you would likely struggle to see it because it is so close to the Sun's position.
